root_cause.text: The netfilter NAT hook registration/unregistration code freed `nf_hook_ops`/private hook storage immediately with `kfree` even though the nfnetlink hook-dump subsystem can still access those RCU-published hook structures, causing a use-after-free due to missing RCU-deferred lifetime management.
root_cause.evidence: The fix replaces `kfree` with `kfree_rcu` for NAT ops in `iptable_nat.c`, `ip6table_nat.c`, and `nf_nat_core.c`, and the commit explicitly says that since v5.14 userspace hook dumping “will peek back into the nf_hook_ops” and that “the nat ops structures have to be deferred too,” including handling “partial exposition of the hooks from error path.”

intent_record.intent_summary: Defer freeing the lookup ops with RCU in the failure path to avoid premature deallocation and potential use-after-free races.
intent_record.what: The error-handling path in ipt_nat_register_lookups() changes the deallocation of the ops object from kfree(ops) to kfree_rcu(ops, rcu).
intent_record.how: At runtime, the ops structure is no longer freed immediately on registration failure; instead it is deferred until after an RCU grace period, preventing potential use-after-free races if the object may still be reachable by RCU readers during unregister/cleanup.

intent_record.intent_summary: Defer freeing NAT lookup ops with RCU to avoid use-after-free races during unregister.
intent_record.what: The code changes the deallocation of `ops` in `ipt_nat_unregister_lookups()` from `kfree(ops)` to `kfree_rcu(ops, rcu)`, using the `rcu` field for deferred freeing.
intent_record.how: Instead of freeing `ops` immediately, the memory is now released only after an RCU grace period, preventing readers still accessing the object under RCU protection from hitting a use-after-free during runtime.

intent_record.intent_summary: Use RCU-delayed freeing for ops in the IPv6 NAT lookup registration error path to avoid freeing memory before RCU readers are done.
intent_record.what: The error-path cleanup in ip6t_nat_register_lookups() was changed from calling kfree(ops) to calling kfree_rcu(ops, rcu) after unregistering previously registered IPv6 NAT functions.
intent_record.how: Instead of freeing the ops object immediately, the code now defers freeing it until after an RCU grace period, preventing potential use-after-free if readers can still access ops through RCU-protected references during or after unregister.

intent_record.intent_summary: Free the IPv6 NAT lookup ops structure via RCU after unregistration to avoid premature deallocation while readers may still access it.
intent_record.what: The deallocation call in ip6t_nat_unregister_lookups() was changed from kfree(ops) to kfree_rcu(ops, rcu), requiring the object to be freed through RCU using its rcu field instead of being freed immediately.
intent_record.how: This delays freeing the ops object until after an RCU grace period, preventing it from being released while concurrent RCU readers may still reference it during or after IPv6 NAT lookup unregistration.

intent_record.intent_summary: Use RCU-deferred freeing for NAT hook private data and ops array on registration failure to avoid concurrent use-after-free bugs.
intent_record.what: In the error path after nf_register_net_hooks(net, nat_ops, ops_count) fails, the code replaces direct freeing of nat_ops[i].priv and nat_ops with an explicit block that assigns nat_ops[i].priv to a local priv variable and frees each entry with kfree_rcu(priv, rcu_head), then frees nat_ops with kfree_rcu(nat_ops, rcu) instead of kfree().
intent_record.how: At runtime, this changes cleanup on hook registration failure from immediate deallocation to RCU-deferred deallocation, preventing memory from being freed while it may still be visible to RCU readers and avoiding potential use-after-free races in concurrent execution.

intent_record.intent_summary: Defer freeing NAT hook operations with RCU during unregister to prevent use-after-free races with concurrent readers.
intent_record.what: The code changes the deallocation of `nat_ops` in `nf_nat_unregister_fn()` from `kfree(nat_ops)` to `kfree_rcu(nat_ops, rcu)` after setting `nat_proto_net->nat_hook_ops = NULL`.
intent_record.how: At runtime, this defers freeing `nat_ops` until after an RCU grace period instead of releasing it immediately, preventing concurrent RCU readers from accessing freed memory and avoiding a potential use-after-free during NAT hook unregistration.

Author: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>

    netfilter: nf_nat: add nat hook register functions to nf_nat
    
    This adds the infrastructure to register nat hooks with the nat core
    instead of the netfilter core.
    
    nat hooks are used to configure nat bindings.  Such hooks are registered
    from ip(6)table_nat or by the nftables core when a nat chain is added.

bic_trace_step.reason: The diff shows the full registration/unregistration lifetime management for the new NAT hook infrastructure, which is sufficient to assess the RCU lifetime issue. The vulnerable construct is present in `nf_nat_unregister_fn()`: when `nat_proto_net->users == 0`, it calls `nf_unregister_net_hooks(net, nat_ops, ops_count);`, then frees each per-hook private object with `kfree_rcu(priv, rcu_head);`, but finally frees the hook ops array itself immediately with `kfree(nat_ops);`. The root cause states that `nf_hook_ops` and related private hook storage were freed immediately even though nfnetlink hook-dump can still access RCU-published hook structures. Here, `nat_proto_net->nat_hook_ops` points to the allocated `nat_ops = kmemdup(orig_nat_ops, ...)`, and those `nf_hook_ops` are released with plain `kfree(nat_ops)` rather than RCU-deferred freeing. Also, registration publishes RCU-visible state via `priv->entries` using `nf_hook_entries_insert_raw(&priv->entries, ops);`, and unregistration removes it with `nf_hook_entries_delete_raw(&priv->entries, ops);`, confirming these structures participate in hook publication. While `priv` is deferred with `kfree_rcu`, the `nf_hook_ops` array is not, so the fix is not present. Therefore this commit version introduces the vulnerable lifetime handling.
